issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, sexual-violence comments as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless the index event also involved sexual assault or closely related content; nothing else in the profile supports that connection.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal of betrayal by a trusted person is difficult to fit with terrorism as the trauma type unless there was a clear interpersonal betrayal component; the rest of the selected items describe loss of control, helplessness, avoidance, dissociation, and substance use rather than interpersonal betrayal.

vignette: When the campus auditorium erupted in a sudden, deafening volley of gunfire, Ajay-then a 37-year-old clinical psychologist teaching at the university-felt the world tilt. The roar cut through his lecture, the audience's startled screams, and the frantic scramble to the exits. In that instant he was suddenly powerless, the sound of the gunshots echoing in a darkness that seemed to swallow the lights. He was certain that he had lost all control, and that the darkness outside the auditorium was an indifferent, threatening void. Those raw sensations-an unending sense of loss of control, the unsettling hush of night, and the metallic ring of gunfire-became the triggers that would later haunt him whenever he heard a sudden noise, felt the darkness of night fall over his apartment, or simply woke to a quiet, empty room. The next weeks were a series of small, self-imposed retreats. After hearing the echo of a distant siren, he avoided the usual stressors of his job: he skipped meetings, turned down invitations to discuss research, and refrained from engaging with students whose anxious questions made his heart race. When the night fell and the house grew still, he slipped into a fantasy world of his own, letting his mind wander to calmer, safer settings. When the triggers resurfaced-whether the night's silence or the faint click of a phone-the only relief he found was in alcohol or the over-prescribed sleep medication he took in an attempt to quiet the rumbling thoughts. In each case, the triggers directly led him to these maladaptive strategies: avoidance, fantasy escape, and substance use. The more he turned to these tactics, the more he felt that the world was a dangerous place, that he could not protect himself, and that the man he had become was no longer recognizable to him. The experience of gunshots and the ensuing chaos had left him with a belief that bad things could not be stopped, and every echo of fear reinforced that helplessness. In time, these negative appraisals spiraled into a deeper reliance on avoidance. The conviction that the world was unsafe made every potential source of stress a threat, so he began to stay home more, shutting out colleagues and friends. The sense of helplessness tightened its grip: each day he spent alone, he imagined a new threat lurking in the quiet. This self-reinforcing loop of fear and avoidance cemented the belief that the world was dangerous, and it made the fantasy escapes and substances feel like the only viable options to survive. The more he withdrew, the more he convinced himself that nothing could be done, and his sense of self deteriorated as he slipped further from the psychologist he had once been. The maladaptive coping methods did not merely sit beside the triggers-they fed them. When he avoided the office, he missed the brief conversations that might have helped him process the day's events, and the silence allowed the triggers to persist unchallenged. The substance use, in particular, blurred his memories of the bombing, making the gunshots feel more distant, but also less real-so that when a sudden noise did occur, it felt like a new, unexplained terror. The fantasy worlds he inhabited were not merely escapes; they were the only places where the darkness did not threaten him, and that, in turn, made the real world seem even more perilous. Each cycle of avoidance and fantasy escape tightened the loop, pulling him further from the social supports that might have provided a sense of safety. The consequences of this cycle were visible in the office. Ajay stopped engaging with patients in a way that felt authentic, his clinical hand becoming detached; he began to see colleagues as potential threats, and the collaborative spirit of his department dulled. At home, his wife noticed that he was less present, that his laughter was rare, and that he often spoke of a world that had turned hostile overnight. He had begun to feel as if he were no longer the person he recognized, a notion that filled him with dread. The very act of asking for help-calling a mental health hotline, arranging an appointment with a therapist-was the first step toward breaking the chain. Ajay is most afraid that he will never regain the sense of control that once defined his profession, but he is hopeful that with therapy he might learn to confront the dark nights and gunshot memories rather than flee from them.
